content: 1. Report all clinically significant post-vaccination reactions to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) at vaers.hhs.gov or by calling 800-822-7967. 2. For vaccine injury compensation inquiries, visit hrsa.gov/vaccinecompensation or call 800-338-2382. 3. For additional information, contact the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services at 202-357-6400 during business hours (Monday–Friday, excluding holidays). 4. The recommendations in this schedule were approved by the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP), the American College of Physicians (ACP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the American College of Nurse-Midwives (ACNM). Vaccine Administration Guidelines: 5. Vaccines are recommended for adults aged 19 years and older based on age groups and medical indications as of February 2016. 6. A vaccine series does not need to be restarted, regardless of the time elapsed between doses. 7. Licensed combination vaccines may be used when any component is indicated, provided no contraindications exist for the other components. Tetanus, Diphtheria, and Pertussis (Td/Tdap) Vaccination: 8. Adults with an unknown or incomplete history of a 3-dose primary series with Td-containing vaccines should begin or complete the series, including a Tdap dose. 9. For unvaccinated adults, administer the first two doses at least 4 weeks apart, and the third dose 6–12 months after the second. 10. Administer a dose of Tdap regardless of the interval since the last tetanus or diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine. 11. Adults should receive a Td booster every 10 years after the initial Tdap dose. Varicella Vaccination: 12. Adults without evidence of immunity to varicella should receive two doses of the single-antigen varicella vaccine or a second dose if they have received only one dose. 13. Pregnant women should be assessed for varicella immunity. Those without immunity should receive the first dose postpartum before discharge and the second dose 4–8 weeks later. Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccination: 14. Females aged 11–26 years should receive a 3-dose series of 2vHPV, 4vHPV, or 9vHPV. 15. Males aged 11–21 years should receive a 3-dose series of 4vHPV or 9vHPV, with vaccination optional for males aged 22–26 years. 16. HPV vaccination is recommended for men who have sex with men and immunocompromised individuals (including those with HIV) through age 26 if not previously vaccinated. 17. The second dose should be administered 4–8 weeks after the first, and the third dose 16 weeks after the second (minimum intervals apply). 18. HPV vaccines are not recommended during pregnancy, but no intervention is needed if pregnancy occurs after initiating the series. The remaining doses should be delayed until after pregnancy. Zoster Vaccination: 19. A single dose of zoster vaccine is recommended for adults aged 60 years and older, regardless of prior herpes zoster episodes. 20. While the vaccine is FDA-approved for individuals aged 50 years and older, ACIP recommends starting at age 60. 21. Adults aged 60 years and older with chronic medical conditions may be vaccinated unless contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy or severe immunodeficiency). Measles, Mumps, and Rubella (MMR) Vaccination: 22. Adults born before 1957 are generally considered immune to measles and mumps. 23. Adults born in 1957 or later should have documentation of at least one dose of MMR vaccine unless contraindicated or laboratory evidence of immunity exists. 24. Provider-diagnosed disease is not acceptable evidence of immunity for measles, mumps, or rubella. Pneumococcal Vaccination: 25. Administer PPSV23 to adults with chronic conditions (e.g., heart disease, lung disease, liver disease, diabetes, alcoholism, or smoking). 26. At age 65 or older, administer PCV13 at least one year after PPSV23, followed by another dose of PPSV23 at least one year after PCV13 and five years after the last PPSV23 dose. 27. Routine pneumococcal vaccination is not recommended for American Indian/Alaska Native adults unless they have specific indications, but public health authorities may recommend it in high-risk areas. Hepatitis A Vaccination: 28. Administer a 2-dose series of single-antigen hepatitis A vaccine (Havrix or Vaqta) or a 3-dose series of combined hepatitis A and B vaccine (Twinrix) to at-risk individuals. 29. For international adoptees, administer the first dose as soon as adoption is planned, ideally two or more weeks before the adoptee’s arrival. Hepatitis B Vaccination: 30. Administer a 3-dose series of hepatitis B vaccine to unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated individuals. 31. The second dose should be given at least one month after the first, and the third dose at least two months after the second (and at least four months after the first). 32. For hemodialysis patients or immunocompromised individuals, administer higher doses or additional doses as recommended. Meningococcal Vaccination: 33. First-year college students aged 21 years or younger living in residence halls should receive a single dose of MenACWY if not previously vaccinated after age 16. 34. Young adults aged 16–23 years may receive a MenB vaccine series for short-term protection against serogroup B meningococcal disease. Haemophilus Influenzae Type b (Hib) Vaccination: 35. Administer one dose of Hib vaccine to adults with anatomical or functional asplenia, sickle cell disease, or those undergoing elective splenectomy if not previously vaccinated. 36. Vaccinate hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients with a 3-dose regimen 6–12 months post-transplant, regardless of prior vaccination history. 37. Hib vaccination is not recommended for adults with HIV infection due to low risk of Hib disease. General Guidance for Immunocompromised Individuals: 38. Inactivated vaccines (e.g., pneumococcal, meningococcal, and inactivated influenza vaccines) are generally acceptable, while live vaccines should be avoided in individuals with immune deficiencies or immunocompromising conditions.
